extracted.intended_audience: Registered patent practitioners (agents and attorneys) who practice before the USPTO, and their supervisors/practice managers
extracted.subtask_description: USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct and supervisory/ethical obligations for practitioners who prepare, file, and supervise patent matters for clients, including standards for communication, conflicts, third‑party payments, supervision of nonpractitioners, and sanctions for violations. The document is a Final Order applying those standards to specific misconduct facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.102(c) — Limiting scope of representation only with informed consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners may provide a limited scope of representation only if the limitation is reasonable and the client gives informed consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations noted: not informing inventors of the scope of representation; not communicating adequate information about the material risks of, and reasonably available alternatives to, limited scope representation; failing to personally obtain informed consent to limit representation (e.g., filing an application but not prosecuting it without client consent).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 — Reasonable diligence and promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with reasonable diligence and promptness when representing clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations: intentionally delaying filing completed applications because of a fee dispute with a third party; failing to timely file applications, resulting in potential harm under first‑inventor‑to‑file rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(2) — Reasonable consultation about means to accomplish client's objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must reasonably consult with clients about the means by which the client's objectives are to be accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations: failing to consult at the beginning of representation about the scope of the invention, failing to consult about the most appropriate type of patent application (provisional, utility, design) for the invention, and failing to discuss filing options when applications are ready but delayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) — Keep client reasonably informed about status
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must keep clients reasonably informed about the status of a matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations: not personally answering clients' questions about applications; not informing clients who filed provisionals of critical filing dates; failing to inform clients that applications were ready to be filed or were intentionally being withheld; misrepresenting status to clients (saying work was being finalized when filing was intentionally delayed).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b) — Explain matters sufficiently for informed decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit a client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations: not explaining differences between application types; not discussing the scope of clients' inventions; not advising on the best form of protection; not explaining material risks/alternatives associated with third‑party payment arrangements or limited scope representations; not explaining options for filing in light of first‑inventor‑to‑file.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.105(b) — Communicate scope of representation and basis of fee
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must communicate the scope of representation and the basis or rate of the fee (preferably in writing) before or within a reasonable time after commencing representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations: failing to send engagement letters explaining scope of representation; failing to communicate the basis of the fee the client paid and amounts the practitioner received from third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.107(a)(2) — Avoid representation when personal interest materially limits the representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not represent a client if there is a significant risk that the representation will be materially limited by the practitioner's personal interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations: representing inventors who are referred by companies that pay substantial referral fees to the practitioner, without disclosing how those financial interests may materially limit the practitioner's ability to represent the client independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.108(f) — Accepting compensation from third parties only with client's informed consent and without interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not accept compensation from one other than the client for representing a client unless: (1) the client gives informed consent; (2) there is no interference with the practitioner's independence of professional judgment or with the client‑practitioner relationship; and (3) information relating to the representation is protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations: accepting payment from invention development companies without informing clients; failing to explain the material risks and alternatives to being paid by a third party; allowing third‑party payments to interfere with independent judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.501 & 11.503 — Managerial and supervisory obligations to ensure compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who are managers or supervisors must make reasonable efforts to ensure that other practitioners and nonpractitioners under their supervision conform to the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations: not implementing effective review procedures to ensure all applications filed were reviewed by a registered practitioner; employing nonpractitioner contractors whose work was filed without appropriate practitioner review; failing to take reasonable steps to ensure nonpractitioners' conduct was compatible with professional obligations; ratifying or being responsible for subordinate violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to review all patent filings before submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Supervising practitioners must review patent searches, patent applications, and responses to Office actions prepared by nonpractitioners before those documents are filed with the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete facts noted: practitioner was responsible for reviewing all patent searches and applications but acknowledged not all applications drafted by nonpractitioners were reviewed prior to filing; lack of review procedures led to violations under supervisory rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.504(b) — Prohibition on forming a de facto partnership with nonpractitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not form a de facto partnership with a nonpractitioner if the partnership's activities consist of the practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations: effectively practicing in partnership with invention development companies (nonpractitioners) that controlled aspects of the legal services provided to inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.504(c) — Prohibition on permitting third parties to direct or regulate professional judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not permit a person who recommends, employs, or pays the practitioner to render legal services for another to direct or regulate the practitioner's independent professional judgment in rendering such services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations: allowing invention development companies to decide the type of application to file and when; complying with instructions to have minimal contact with clients; permitting companies to limit scope of representation or interfere with prosecution decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.505 — Prohibition on assisting another in unauthorized practice of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not assist nonpractitioners in engaging in the unauthorized practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations: allowing nonregistered salespeople at invention development companies to advise inventors about patent law matters (scope of inventions, meaning of provisional/utility/design applications, which application to purchase); preparing prior art reports containing 'suitability' and 'chances of approval' statements that nonpractitioners used to sell patent application packages.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) — Prohibition on misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not engage in conduct involving a misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations: making incorrect statements to clients and to OED (e.g., denying that applications were withheld or work stopped due to fee disputes when email evidence showed otherwise).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i) — Conduct that adversely reflects on fitness to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must avoid engaging in conduct that adversely reflects on their fitness to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order cites conduct (communications, supervisory failures, conflicts) that reflect adversely on fitness to practice and are subject to disciplinary action and public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to disclose financial arrangements and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must disclose to clients material financial arrangements and potential conflicts (e.g., referral fees received from third parties) that could affect representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/violations: failing to inform clients that practitioner received hundreds of thousands of dollars from invention development company referrals; failing to explain the potential conflict arising from the practitioner's personal financial interest in continued referrals; failing to obtain informed client consent for such arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty not to delay filings for third parties without client consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not withhold filing of clients' completed patent applications due to disputes with third‑party payors without informing clients and consulting on potential harm and options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts noted: practitioner withheld filing due to unpaid invoices from an invention development company, did not inform inventors their applications were ready but being held, and did not consult about harm or alternatives — violating duties of diligence, communication, and explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions and conditions for reinstatement (Final Order specifics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary sanctions imposed and specific conditions for reinstatement following suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreed sanctions in this case: suspension from practice in patent matters for 48 months (with petition for reinstatement permitted after 42 months but not granted before 48 months); require, as conditions of reinstatement, to (1) take the MPRE and attain a score of 85 or better and provide corroborating declaration; (2) attend or audit a continuing legal education/ethics class on conflicts of interest, supervising employees, or trust accounts and provide corroborating declaration; comply with 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58 and 11.60; limited recognition granted for 30 days solely to facilitate compliance with § 11.58; submit a supplemental affidavit no sooner than 47 months and 3 weeks after the Final Order attesting compliance with § 11.58; the OED Director will publish the Final Order and a materially consistent notice in the Official Gazette.
